title: Momentum: The Quantity of Motion
hook: A slow freight train and a fast bullet are both brutally hard to stop. Momentum captures why: it's mass times velocity, the real measure of moving 'oomph'.
key_points: Momentum is mass times velocity — the 'quantity of motion' an object carries.
Heavy or fast objects have lots of it and are hard to stop or deflect.
Changing momentum takes a force applied over time, called impulse.
Impulse is the truest statement of Newton's second law: force changes momentum.
content_html: Momentum is a measure of how much motion an object has — formally, its mass multiplied by its velocity. It's why a slow-moving truck and a speeding bullet are both hard to stop: the truck has huge mass, the bullet has huge speed, and either way the product is large. Momentum has direction, too, pointing the way the object moves.
extra_html: To change an object's momentum you have to apply a force, and the longer that force acts, the bigger the change. That product of force and time is called impulse, and it's actually how Newton originally framed his second law: force is the rate at which momentum changes. This is the physics behind crumple zones and airbags — they don't reduce how much your momentum must change in a crash, but by stretching the collision over more time they shrink the force you feel. Wikipedia traces the definition of momentum and its link to impulse and Newton's laws.

related.title: Newton's Three Laws of Motion
related.hook: Three short rules — inertia, F=ma, and action-reaction — quietly govern almost everything that moves around you.

related.title: Conservation of Momentum
related.hook: Fire a gun and it kicks back; push off a friend on skates and you both glide apart. Total momentum never changes unless an outside force interferes.

flashcards.back_html: Momentum is an object's mass times its velocity. It measures how much motion an object has and how hard it is to stop.

flashcards.prompt: Why does a car airbag reduce injury in a crash?

choices.text: It stretches the stop over more time, so the force needed to change your momentum is smaller
It adds momentum to cancel yours out

flashcards.explanation_html: The same change in momentum spread over a longer time means a gentler force — that's impulse, force times time.

flashcards.prompt: Which has more momentum: a heavy truck creeping along, or a light pebble at the same slow speed?

choices.text: The truck — more mass means more momentum at the same velocity
The pebble, because it's easier to throw
They have equal momentum at equal speed

flashcards.explanation_html: Momentum is mass times velocity, so for the same speed the heavier object carries far more momentum.
